name: World Vision US: domestic programmes (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: donated goods passed to US churches, schools and nonprofits.
summary: World Vision US's domestic programmes ($231 million in fiscal 2025) pass donated corporate goods (clothing, household goods, school and building supplies: $163 million at wholesale value) to US churches, schools and nonprofits from its warehouses. Valued on the site's one log-income scale at low-income Americans' consumption, at 60% of their recorded value as goods given in kind, a dollar does about 0.004 years of healthy life per $1,000, far below the global-health median because the goods go to people in a rich country, where they add little to consumption, not because the work is badly run. World Vision US publishes no count of the households its goods reach, so reach is the goods' value over a judged amount per household and the model is discounted for missing data; the biggest uncertainties are what the goods are worth to families and how many would have reached them anyway.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Domestic programmes, fiscal 2025

rows.explainer: World Vision US's total functional expenses, fiscal 2025 (Form 990 Part IX).

rows.explainer: All three programme lines, same statement.

rows.label: Overhead multiplier (total ÷ program expenses)
rows.explainer: World Vision US's management and fundraising spread over its programmes by cost, as in its international model.

rows.label: Cost of the modelled program, including overhead
rows.explainer: The domestic line plus its share of overhead. The donated goods are in it at the wholesale value World Vision records them at.

rows.label: Donated goods passed to US partners, fiscal 2025
rows.explainer: Household goods, clothing, toys, building supplies, hygiene and school supplies at wholesale value (Schedule M lists $189.0M of clothing and household goods received, $22.3M building supplies, $19.3M toys, $3.2M school supplies, part of them sent abroad).

rows.label: Goods value per household reached in a year (wholesale)
rows.explainer: World Vision US publishes no count of the US households its goods reach. Partners hand out a few bags of clothing, hygiene kits, school supplies or household goods per family; building supplies for home repairs and disaster recovery go to fewer households at higher value. Judgment $180 a household a year ($60-500).

rows.label: Households reached in the year
rows.explainer: Goods passed to partners over the value per household: about 900,000 households at the best guesses.

rows.label: People per household
rows.explainer: The site's US household size: families with children are the main recipients (school supplies, clothing), larger than the poorest fifth's average of 1.6.

rows.label: People reached
rows.explainer: People reached.

rows.label: Cost per person reached
rows.explainer: Context.

rows.label: Life-satisfaction gain per person-year
rows.explainer: 0: the goods' value is counted below as income; counting their relief as wellbeing too would count it twice.

rows.label: Years the wellbeing effect lasts
rows.explainer: Not used (no wellbeing effect counted).

rows.label: WELLBYs per person
rows.explainer: Point-years, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: What the goods are worth to the family, as a share of their wholesale value
rows.explainer: Corporate surplus goods given in kind: families can't choose what they get, some items go unused, and wholesale value is below what a family would pay at discount retail. Anchored on the literature valuing in-kind transfers (80-95% of face value for food stamps, less for goods the family wouldn't have bought) and on the Salvation Army model's 80% for food and clothing it picks: 60% (40-85%).

rows.label: Value of the goods to each person, per year (US$)
rows.explainer: About $45 a person a year at the best guesses.

rows.label: US consumption per person (Consumer Expenditure Survey)
rows.explainer: The site's US survey consumption per person.

rows.label: Recipients' consumption per person, as a share of the US average
rows.explainer: Partners serve low-income families, schools in poor districts (Title I) and disaster-hit households: about the poorest fifth, whose household spending is 45% of the average (@united_states.ce_lowest_quintile_vs_all_2024; per person higher, as poorer households are smaller, but these are families with children). Judgment 45% (30-70%).

rows.label: Recipients' consumption per person per year
rows.explainer: Recipients' consumption per person per year.

rows.label: Years the gain counts
rows.explainer: 1: a year's goods.

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per person
rows.explainer: The site's one log-income scale at the recipients' own consumption.

rows.label: Health gained per person (DALYs)
rows.explainer: 0: no evidence that donated household goods, clothing or supplies change health in the US.

rows.label: Deaths averted per person
rows.explainer: 0: none expected from these goods.

rows.label: Share of deaths under five (not used)
rows.explainer: No deaths averted are counted.

rows.label: Share of deaths 5-14 (not used)
rows.explainer: No deaths averted are counted.

rows.label: Share of deaths 15-49 (not used)
rows.explainer: No deaths averted are counted.

rows.label: Value of a death averted
rows.explainer: GiveWell's moral weights by the age band of each death, times your value of a life: the site's one value of a death.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: The value is the goods at a judged share of their recorded value, which needs no effect study; 0.95 (0.8-1) for valuations that may not match what was given.

rows.label: Share of the goods families wouldn't have got anyway
rows.explainer: Without World Vision, much corporate surplus would still reach families through other in-kind charities (Good360, food banks' non-food lines) or discount sale; some would be destroyed. 65% (40-90%).

rows.label: World Vision's share of the resources behind the goods reaching families
rows.explainer: The goods are in World Vision's cost; partner churches and schools add volunteer time and space to hand them out (World Vision US counts 28,224 volunteers across all its work, 990 Part I). 85% (70-95%).

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Share of the goods that reach families and get used
rows.explainer: Some goods sit in partners' storage, go unused or are passed on. 85% (70-95%).

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: The goods are donated; cash pays for the logistics that bring them in, so a dollar's leverage is in the goods' value already. 1 (0.95-1.05).

rows.label: Missing-data discount
rows.explainer: Thin: World Vision US publishes no count of the households its US goods reach; reach and value are judgments. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.formula: evidence_adj * counterfactual_adj * attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Not modelled: home repairs that last more than a year and disaster-recovery supplies (+), teachers' time saved and school attendance (+); goods that displace local purchases from small shops (-). +5% (-5% to +20%).
